newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Aid chiefs still unsure if troops needed in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Aid chiefs still unsure if troops needed in Zaire.

text.p: Aid officials ended one-day talks on central Africa's refugee crisis on Saturday still apparently disagreeing how many refugees are on the move, where they are and whether foreign troops should go in.
They offered no united view on plans for a U.N. international force to help agencies get relief to wandering refugees in eastern Zaire.
But they urged Rwandan and Zairean governments and ethnic Tutsi rebels, who seized large swathes of east Zaire in a lightning offensive last month, to cooperate with relief efforts.

"It's still necessary to provide aid to the refugees. But no one wants a military force to go there for no reason," Canada's international cooperation minister Don Boudria, who chaired the meeting behind closed doors, told a news briefing.
"If people allow that aid to go in by other means, that's fine."

The return to Rwanda this week of 500,000 Hutus, among one million refugees in east Zaire who fled Rwanda after 1994's Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis, has shifted the thrust of Western relief efforts to Rwanda, Africa's most crowded country.
It has also weakened support for a planned multinational task force in east Zaire -- an idea vehemently opposed by Rwanda's new Tutsi rulers, who swept to power after the genocide.
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, expressed frustration with the long series of meetings and delays in mounting the Canadian-led multinational force.
"There are many conferences. I don't know which one ties up with which one," she told reporters.

"We have no access (to refugees in eastern Zaire). I think the international community and those who have the capacity to move in with various advanced modern technology would probably be able to give us access."
Rwanda, which has refused to let Western powers mount a military operation from its soil, for its part put a $700 million price tag on its efforts to resettle refugees.

"We have made an assessment of needs for speedy resettlement and reintegration of refugees. We need around $700 million," Charles Murigande, head of Rwanda's government delegation and transport and telecommunications minister, told reporters.
"The main elements are emergency need for food and quick assistance. But housing is the major aspect," he said.

Disagreement between the U.S. government, the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR and several other agencies over the number of refugees in eastern Zaire has complicated talks over what kind of relief should be sent and where.
Washington's top aid official, U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) chief Brian Atwood, said military planning was hampered by the fluid situation.

He said: "There is a great deal of uncertainty about the situation in eastern Zaire. There is an awful lot of movement that is contributing to the uncertainty about military planning in this region. There is also continuing conflict."
"The call for the combatants and the governments of the region to provide access to this region...was an important message and an urgent appeal," Atwood added.
Atwood said the U.S. government estimated there were around 400,000 refugees in the region. The UNHCR says there are 700,000 while Rwanda claims there are hardly any refugees left at all.
He said recent U.S. aerial surveys of eastern Zaire had not always proved fully reliable.

"Aerial reconnaisance of the type that has been undertaken is a very imperfect science," he said. "We see groups of people one day, we don't see them the next because of cloud cover. Or we may back to the same area and see that they've disappeared."
